stories.headline: A 71,677-PR study complicates claims about coding-agent quality

source.title: How do teams evaluate code changes attributed to AI agents?
source.scope: Reviewed the full paper across 71,677 pull requests and six agents, including attribution limits, merge outcomes, review allocation, model features and the authors’ noncausal limitations.
source.freshness_reason: Within 168 hours; selected as a justified scientific-paper fallback because it supplies unique large-sample evidence about review and merge outcomes.

read_evidence.scope: Reviewed the full paper across 71,677 pull requests and six agents, including attribution limits, merge outcomes, review allocation, model features and the authors’ noncausal limitations.

stories.summary: Researchers analyzed 71,677 pull requests attributed to six coding agents. Pooled coauthored changes merged less often than agent-only changes, but removing one dominant agent reversed that pattern, exposing composition effects. Adding context features improved reported merge prediction from 0.774 to 0.832 AUC. The observational study does not establish that any review practice caused acceptance.
stories.why_it_matters: Engineering leaders should not compare agent merge rates without agent mix, repository context and attribution rules. Track review depth, requested changes and final disposition separately, then test whether an intervention improves outcomes rather than reading causality into retrospective correlations.
stories.related_coverage: Selected after the owner-directed Watchlist lead was traced to the original paper and evaluated against current engineering evidence.
stories.image_alt_intent: Thousands of coding-agent pull requests flow through separate review, revision and merge lanes, with a warning that composition can reverse an aggregate conclusion.

coverage_labels: Applied Generative AI for Knowledge Workers
stories.summary: Gallup surveyed 21,648 U.S. employees in August and found 32% used AI frequently. Among frequent users, 52% reported spending less time gathering information and 47% less time writing, while meetings were largely unchanged. These are self-reported task shifts, not measured productivity. A separate field experiment provides different evidence and should not be blended.
